abertura: One of the two texts you will read was written by a person who was there. The other was written by someone who arrived afterwards and wrote down what he was told.
Mark the two statements that are true of a **witness account** and not of an incident report.

itens.t: It is written by someone who saw what happened.
It is written to a fixed form, with headings and times.
It can say what the person felt or thought at the moment.
It is signed by the officer on duty.
It is the same on every night of the year.

sec1.rationale: An account is one person's version. A report is a record made to a form -- it can be complete and still leave out what only the witness could know.

nota.texto: Both texts will disagree with each other tonight. Neither of them is lying: they were written by different people, for different purposes, at different hours.

abertura: Choose the better meaning for each expression. You will meet all six in the two texts.

itens.t: an account
alts: the official decision about what happened
one person's version of what happened
itens.ok: one person's version of what happened

itens.t: to claim
alts: to say something is true without proving it
to say something after checking it
itens.ok: to say something is true without proving it

itens.t: to state
alts: to say it clearly, and on the record
itens.ok: to say it clearly, and on the record

itens.t: to leave something out
alts: to not mention it at all
to say it in fewer words
itens.ok: to not mention it at all

itens.t: consistent with
as far as I can tell
alts: this is my reading, and I could be wrong
itens.ok: this is my reading, and I could be wrong

nota.titulo: Two of these do the work
nota.texto: Two of these do the work of the whole lesson: claim and state. What a text *states* you can point to. What someone *claims* you can only attribute -- and that is a different sentence.

abertura: Six statements. Say which text supports each one -- and notice that one of them is supported by neither.

doc.titulo: Witness account · Ms. Ferraz · Incident report · Officer on duty
doc.texto:
**Ferraz:** I got home a little before eleven. There were four of them on the corner, and one of them called out to me first -- I did not speak until he did. I did not see anyone leave.

**Report:** Attendance recorded at 23:40. Three individuals present at the location. The complainant states that she addressed the group. No mention of any individual leaving the scene.

itens.t: Someone in the group spoke before she did.
There were three people on the corner.
Nobody is recorded as leaving the scene.
She was frightened by the group.
The time is close to eleven at night.
She spoke to the group first.

nota.titulo: “She was frightened” is the one to hold on to
nota.texto:
Both texts put the hour near eleven — they do not disagree about when, only about how exactly. On who spoke first they say opposite things: that is a real divergence.

And she was frightened is in neither. It is the kind of thing a reader adds without noticing, because it fits. Saying it out loud as if it came from the account is the mistake this lesson is built to catch.

abertura: Mark the two things you cannot get from either text.

itens.t: Why the group was on that corner.
How many people the report recorded.
What was said after the first words.
What time the officer recorded.
Whether the witness spoke first.

sec4.rationale: Two texts that disagree are still two texts. What both of them leave out is not a divergence -- it is a hole, and it is the thing worth asking for.

nota.titulo: The hole is not a divergence
nota.texto: In class you will report the divergences. The strongest briefings end with the hole, not with the last divergence.

abertura: Each sentence reports something. Complete it so that the source is attached to the claim.

itens.t: The report records three people;
She was not the first to speak --
On the time,
alts: the two are close but not identical
itens.ok: the two are close but not identical

itens.t: Neither text mentions why the group was there,
alts: so we would need to ask
itens.ok: so we would need to ask

nota.texto: Notice what the rejected endings do: they turn a report into a verdict. *Four is the correct number* is not reading -- it is deciding, and nobody asked you to decide yet.

abertura: Complete the paragraph. Every gap is one of the six expressions from activity 2.
itens: The witness {account|150px} says four people were on the corner; the report {states|150px} three.
She {claims|140px} that one of them spoke first, and the report says the opposite.
Both texts {leave out|150px} the reason the group was there.
On the hour, the two are broadly {consistent with|180px} each other.
{As far as I can tell|190px}, the difference that matters is who spoke first.
banco: as far as I can tell

nota.texto: This paragraph is the skeleton of the briefing you will give in class. If you can write it, you can say it — and in class you will say it without the text in front of you.

abertura: A quick reference to the situation and the language you used.

tabela: A three-minute briefing to someone who has read neither of two accounts of the same incident.
Naming where the two stop agreeing, and saying which account each claim comes from.
According to the witness account… · The report states… · That comes from her, not from the record.
These two do not line up on… · She claims X; the report says Y.
As far as I can tell… · That is my reading, not what either text says.
Neither account mentions… · That is what I would want to ask.

abertura: Record a short voice message, if you would like to.

callout.texto:
Think of two accounts of the same event in your own work — two witnesses, a statement and a record, a version told in the hearing and a version told before it.

What you are trying to do: tell a colleague where the two stop agreeing, in a way she could repeat to someone else without reading either one.

lista: what each account is, and who wrote it;
the one divergence that changes something;
one thing neither of them says.

callout.texto: A colleague from another country asks you, in writing, what the disagreement was about. She has read neither account.

abertura: Keep the source attached to every claim. If something is your reading and not the text's, say so.
Written in plain English, about the thing this lesson turned on: two people describing the same night differently.

itens.titulo: How Eyewitness Misidentification Can Send Innocent People to Prison
itens.texto: Why two honest accounts of the same event diverge, and what the divergence is worth in a case. Short, free, and written for the general reader.

abertura: Two talks on the same question, from opposite sides. Both have full transcripts and subtitles.

itens.texto: A memory researcher on why a confident account and an accurate account are not the same thing. Slow, clear delivery — good listening practice at your level.
A forensic expert reconstructs one night from conflicting accounts. It is the operation of this lesson, done at full length by someone who does it for a living.

saysource.titulo: Attaching a claim to its source
abertura: Three things a sentence can do with a claim, and the words that do each one.

tabela:
The report states three individuals. · According to the account, there were four.
You can put a finger on the line. Nobody has to trust you.

She claims that he spoke first. · That comes from her, not from the record.
The claim stays hers. You are reporting, not endorsing.

As far as I can tell, the hour is not the problem.
The moment you drop this, your reading starts sounding like the document's.

callout.texto: The mistake is not saying something false — it is saying something true in the sentence that belongs to a document. She was frightened may well be right. Neither text says it, and in a briefing that difference is the whole of your credibility.

itens.t: Four people were on the corner.
The hour recorded is 23:40.
Nobody is recorded as leaving.
She was frightened by the group.
She addressed the group first.
Someone in the group spoke first.

nota.titulo: Two of these are the lesson
nota.texto: Nobody is recorded as leaving is in both — agreement is a finding too, and briefings that only list disagreements sound like accusations. She was frightened is in neither, and it is the one you will be tempted to say.

opcoes: it is what I would ask for

itens.t: "The two accounts disagree about who spoke first."
"Somebody left before the officer arrived."
"The report records three individuals."
"We need to know why the group was there."
itens.ok: it is what I would ask for

itens.t: "She was not the one who started it."
"The hour is close in both."

nota.titulo: The middle column is where credibility is lost
nota.texto: None of the three is wrong to say. What is wrong is saying the second kind in the sentence that belongs to the first — somebody left with the intonation of the report records three. In a briefing, the person listening cannot tell which one you meant unless you mark it.
